name: Liability

subjectOf.text: Artificial intelligence cannot be held personally liable for damage it causes because national and international law do not currently recognize it as a subject of law, so compensation must be forced through existing provisions never designed for it.
subjectOf.abstract: However, national and international law do not (currently) recognize AI as a subject of law. Without legal personality, AI cannot be personally liable for damages.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477
scope_conditions: current state of national and international law

subjectOf.text: Because neither national nor international law recognizes artificial intelligence as a subject of law, AI has no legal personality and therefore cannot itself be held liable for the damages it causes.
subjectOf.abstract: Because national and international law do not currently recognize AI as a subject of law, AI has no legal personality and as such cannot be held personally liable for damages.
subjectOf.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: under the legal frameworks in force as of 2017

subjectOf.text: Corporate lawyers and governance experts still discourage executives from communicating in a personalized, speech-like way, particularly on social media, out of fear of market misunderstanding and subsequent liability.
subjectOf.abstract: Corporate lawyers and corporate governance experts currently still discourage a more personalized and speech-like way of communicating for corporate executives.
subjectOf.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176

subjectOf.text: There is little or no recourse for clients when reviewed code proves to be flawed even after functionality and quality review.
subjectOf.abstract: Moreover, there is little or no recourse for clients in cases in which the code proved to be flawed even after functionality and quality review.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How DAOs Optimize Open-Source Code Reviews and Create Open-Source Standards (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3995709
scope_conditions: the existing code review and audit market

subjectOf.text: Decentralized organizations carry inherent risks that require establishing a legal entity, and establishing that legal entity inherently contradicts the notion of decentralization.
subjectOf.abstract: Third, decentralized organizations themselves come with inherent risks that require establishing a legal entity, which inherently contradicts the notion of decentralization.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715

subjectOf.text: Clients have little or no recourse when reviewed code turns out to be flawed even after a functionality and quality review has been performed and paid for.
subjectOf.abstract: Moreover, there is little or no recourse for clients in cases in which the code proved to be flawed even after functionality and quality review.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Code Review DAO (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4734750

subjectOf.text: Web3 data attestation supports a governance model that assigns liability for AI misuse to identifiable individuals rather than distributing the burden across the whole community, which is what makes it a workable answer to AI related ethical dilemmas.
subjectOf.abstract: By ensuring accountability at the individual level, rather than burdening the entire community, this proposed model for AI governance within Web3 offers a promising avenue to address ethical dilemmas associated with AI applications.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4796714
scope_conditions: requires cryptographic data attestation and verifiable identity
applies to liability arising from AI misuse and uploaded content

subjectOf.text: DAO-based governance introduces unresolved uncertainty about liability and legal accountability when personal data crosses international boundaries, and a mismatch between platform governance and regulatory mandates produces legal liability that erodes user trust.
subjectOf.abstract: decentralized governance models, such as DAOs, introduce uncertainties regarding liability and legal accountability when personal data is exchanged across international boundaries. A mismatch between platform governance and regulatory mandates can result in legal liabilities, undermining user trust
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Artificial Intelligence The Final Frontier (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5095633

subjectOf.text: Keeping judges ultimately accountable through a human-in-the-loop review of AI generated reasoning, as practiced in Shenzhen, does not fully resolve the accountability problem in AI assisted adjudication.
subjectOf.abstract: Shenzhen case study illustrates that judges retain ultimate accountability, revising AI-generated reasoning to ensure accurate judgments, but this human-in-the-loop approach does not fully resolve the issue.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Morgan A. Gray, The Evolving Role of Artificial Intelligence in Law (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5541658
scope_conditions: judicial settings where AI drafts or supports reasoning that a human judge then reviews
